<noinclude><pagequality level="4" user="Yann" />{{rh|178|AITAREYÂ-ARA''N''YAKA.|}}{{rule}}</noinclude><section begin="aranyaka1 adhyaya3" />intercalating these) he does not begin simply with a ''Rik'', Ya''g''us, or Sâman verse, he does not start with a ''Rik'', a Ya''g''us, or a Sâman  verse.


{{sh|{{sc|{{Anchor+|Khanda3|Third Kha''nd''a}}.}}}}

1. He begins with tad, this, (the first word of the first hymn, {{lang|sa-Latn|tad id âsa}}). Verily 'this, this' is food, 
and thus he obtains food.

2. Pra''g''âpati indeed uttered this as the first word, consisting of one or two syllables, viz. tata and tita (or tat)<ref>Tata and tâta are used both by children in addressing their parents, and by parents in addressing their children. If tat is called the very same word, eva is used in the sense of iva.</ref>. And thus does a child, as soon as he begins to speak, utter the word, consisting of one or two syllables, viz. tata and tita (or tat). With this very word, consisting of tat or tatta, he begins.

3. This has been said by a ''Ri''shi (Rv. X, 71, 1)<ref>The verse is cited to confirm the meaning of tat, the first word 
of the first hymn ({{lang|sa-Latn|tad id âsa}}), as explained before. It was said that tat was the first name applied to a child. Now, according to Â''s''valâyana G''ri''hya-sûtra I, 16, 8, a name is given to a child at the time of its birth, a name which no one knows except father and mother, till the time when he is initiated by a Guru. This is called the abhivadanîya name. In allusion to this custom it is said here that tata is the secret name of the child, which becomes publicly known at a later time only. Of course the interpretation of the verse in that sense is unnatural, but quite in keeping with the general character of the Âra''n''yaka. I doubt whether even the commentator understood what was intended by the author, and whether the gods who enter the body are supposed to know the name, or whether the name refers to these gods, or, it may be, to tad, the Brahman.</ref>:—

4. 'O B''ri''haspati, the first point of speech;'—for this is the first and highest point of speech.

5. 'That which you have uttered, making it a name;'—for names are made by speech.
